title: The Story We Live In: Creation, Fall, Redemption, Restoration
subtitle: Not a set of doctrines to affirm, but a story to live inside. A Christian reckoning with the whole biblical drama in four acts, with why a person cannot live well without a true story to inhabit, and with how creation, fall, redemption, and restoration become the frame that holds an integrated life together.

connections.label: The four-act story is the frame the whole integrated vision hangs on. The integrated life has its own page.
The first act, creation, is where our work and our keeping of the world begin. Creation and our keeping has its own page.
Living rightly inside the story is the heart of what it means to follow Jesus. Discipleship has its own page.
The fall and the not-yet are why we still wait in a world not yet made right. Waiting and unanswered prayer has its own page.
The story locates our suffering inside an act that is not the last one. Suffering and the silence of God has its own page.

parts.title: The Person With No Story to Live In
parts.body:
You wake up and the day does not seem to be about anything. You go to the work, answer the messages, feed the children, pay the bills, and somewhere underneath the motion a quiet question runs that you do not say out loud, which is what all of this is for and where it is going. You were handed, by the air you breathe, a thin set of answers. You are here by accident, you are free to write your own meaning, you will end and be forgotten, so make it pleasant while it lasts. And on a good day that is enough to keep you moving. On a hard day, when the diagnosis comes or the marriage cracks or you stand at a grave, it falls apart in your hands, because a story that says your life is an accident headed nowhere cannot carry the weight of a life that actually hurts.

That is the strange poverty of the age that thinks it has outgrown stories. We were told that the old grand narratives were illusions, that the mature mind lives without one, that you are free precisely because no story has a claim on you. And so a generation tries to live with no frame at all, improvising meaning by the day, assembling a self out of fragments, and discovering that a life with no story is not free but disoriented, that you cannot answer the simplest questions of how to live because you do not know what kind of world you are living in, what time it is, or how the story you are inside is meant to end.

Let me name the thing I told myself for years, because it is the most sophisticated lie available. I told myself I did not need a story, that I could face reality clear-eyed without the comfort of a grand narrative, that meaning was a private project I would build myself. And underneath that brave posture I was quietly borrowing a story all along, the thin one the culture had handed me, and living by it without admitting it, and wondering why my courage kept collapsing the moment life grew serious. You cannot actually live without a story. You can only live without knowing which one you are in, which means living by a borrowed one you never examined and cannot defend.

Here is what living storyless does to a person, slowly. It fragments you. Your work means one thing and your faith another and your suffering nothing at all, and there is no frame that holds them together, so you live in pieces, each part of your life unconnected to the rest. You cannot tell whether your pain is meaningful or random, whether your work matters or merely fills the time, whether the world is a gift or an accident, because you have no story large enough to locate any of it. You are a character who does not know what play he is in, improvising lines in the dark, and your disorientation is not a failure of intelligence. It is the inevitable condition of a creature trying to live without the one thing he was made to live inside.

We taught a generation that it could live without a story and then watched it drown in meaninglessness. We called the loss of the grand narrative liberation and could not understand the anxiety, the rootlessness, the quiet despair it produced. The hunger you feel for your life to be about something, to fit inside a larger meaning, to be a chapter in a story going somewhere, is not an immaturity to be outgrown. It is the homesickness of a creature made for a true story and handed only fragments, and the answer is not to kill the hunger but to find the story large enough and true enough to fill it.

parts.title: Why You Cannot Live Well Without a True Story
parts.body:
It matters because you cannot know how to act until you know what story you are in. The simplest question of how to live well turns out to depend entirely on a prior question, what kind of world is this and how does the story go. If the world is a random accident, then there is no grain to live along, no purpose to honor, and your choices are arbitrary preferences dressed up as meaning. If the world is a gift with a Giver, a story with an Author and an ending, then every choice is a response, a way of living truly or falsely inside a real drama. You cannot derive how to live from nowhere. You can only derive it from the story you believe you are inside, which means the story is not decoration laid over your ethics. It is the foundation underneath them.

It matters because the fragments of a life only hold together inside a frame, and the four-act story is the frame. Your work, your marriage, your money, your suffering, your body, your death, are not separate problems to be solved one at a time. They are all chapters of a single story, and only the story holds them together. Take the story away and the integrated life is impossible, because there is nothing to integrate around, no center, no plot, no direction. Give the story back and everything finds its place, your work as part of the keeping of creation, your suffering as a chapter inside an act that is not the last one, your death as a comma and not a period. A person living inside the true story is not living a series of disconnected episodes. He is living one coherent life, and the coherence comes entirely from the story.

It matters because the culture that thinks it has escaped all stories is in fact captive to a worse one, and naming the true story is the only way out. The age does not live without a narrative. It lives by a powerful and unexamined one, the story of the autonomous self writing its own meaning in a meaningless universe, free, sovereign, and alone, and that story is producing exactly the anxiety, fragmentation, and quiet despair you would expect from a creature trying to be the author of a play he did not write. The believer who has found the true story is not someone clinging to a comfort. He is someone who has woken up inside the real drama and can see the thin counterfeit for what it is, and his life is a sign held up to a culture that has forgotten there is any other story to live in.

And it matters because the watching skeptic is not finally moved by arguments but by the question of which story can carry a real life. He is not in the room for your doctrine. He is in the room watching whether your story holds when your life breaks, whether the frame you live in can bear a grave, a diagnosis, an injustice, a Tuesday afternoon that has come apart. The thin story of the accidental self has nothing to say at the graveside, and the skeptic knows it, having stood there himself. The four-act story claims to hold all of it, the goodness and the ruin and the rescue and the world set right, and the skeptic is watching to see whether the people who claim that story actually live as though it were true, because a story that can carry a life is the most persuasive thing in the world to a man whose own story has run out.

parts.title: The Drama in Four Acts
parts.body:
Scripture is not first a rulebook or a manual or a collection of timeless principles. It is a story, a single sweeping drama that runs from the first sentence of Genesis to the last vision of Revelation, and it moves in four great acts, creation, fall, redemption, restoration. Miss that it is a story and you will mine it for verses while missing the plot, and a person who has the verses but not the story has the pieces of a play he cannot follow. The Bible asks first not to be agreed with but to be lived inside, the way you live inside a story you have entered and cannot get out of, and its four acts are the frame for everything a human being needs to know about where he is, what went wrong, what is being done about it, and where it is all going.

The first act is creation, and it sets the deepest note, that everything that exists is a gift and that the gift was good. In the beginning God made the heavens and the earth, and at every stage he looked and saw that it was good, and at the end, very good. The world is not an accident and not an illusion and not a prison. It is a made thing, made on purpose, made good, and the human creature is set in it as an image bearer, given work to do, a garden to keep, a partner to love, a Sabbath to rest in. The first act tells you that matter matters, that bodies and work and food and marriage and rest are not distractions from the spiritual life but the very stuff of it, that the world is charged with the goodness of the One who made it. Everything that comes after is haunted by the memory of this goodness, because the ruin is the ruin of something that was once very good, and the rescue is the rescue of a world worth saving.

The second act is the fall, and it is the act that explains why the world you actually live in does not match the goodness you can still feel it was meant for. The human creatures, given everything, reached for the one thing forbidden, grasped at being their own authors, their own gods, and in that grasping the whole creation cracked. The ground is cursed, the work turns to sweat and thorns, the marriage turns to blame, the brother kills the brother, and death enters and spreads to all. The fall is the Bible telling the truth about the brokenness you cannot deny, the gap between the world as it is and the world as you know it ought to be. It refuses both the lie that says everything is fine and the lie that says the world was always a horror. The world is good and the world is broken, both at once, because a good creation has been ruined, and only an account that holds those two together can make sense of a life that is full of glory and full of grief in the same hour.

The third act is redemption, and it is the long turning of the story from ruin toward rescue, the act that fills most of the Bible. God does not abandon the wrecked creation or scrap it and start over. He sets out to redeem it, calling Abraham, forming a people, giving the law, sending the prophets, narrowing the rescue down through a nation and a remnant to a single point, a child in a manger, who is God himself come into his own ruined world to save it from the inside. At the center of the act stands the cross, where the Author writes himself into the story and takes its ruin into his own body, and the empty tomb, where the rescue breaks into the world in advance, the first morning of the new creation rising in the middle of the old. Redemption is not God rescuing souls out of a doomed world. It is God reclaiming the world itself, beginning with a people in whom the rescue has already started, the new creation appearing now in pockets and signs while the old creation still groans around it.

The fourth act is restoration, and it is the ending the whole story has been straining toward, the goal that pulls everything forward. The Bible does not end with souls escaping to a disembodied heaven. It ends with heaven coming down to earth, the new Jerusalem descending, God dwelling with his people, every tear wiped away, death itself destroyed, the whole creation set free from its bondage to decay and made new. The last act is restoration, the good creation of act one not abandoned but healed, the body raised, the world remade, the dwelling of God with man. This is the ending that gives the whole drama its shape, and a Christian lives between the acts, in the strange overlap where redemption has begun and restoration has not yet come, the kingdom already breaking in and not yet here in full, and learning to live in that overlap, sober about the not-yet and certain of the already, is most of what it means to live wisely inside the story.

And the four acts are not finally a structure but a person, because the story has a center and his name is Jesus. He is the one through whom all things were made in act one, the one whose death and resurrection turn act three, the one who will return to complete act four. Every act points to him, gathers around him, finds its meaning in him. To live inside the story is not, in the end, to inhabit a clever framework. It is to know the One who is the story's author and hero and ending all at once, to find your own small life written into his great one, your work part of his keeping, your suffering inside his act of rescue, your death swallowed up in his resurrection, your whole fragmented existence gathered into a single coherent drama because the One who is its center has made you a character in his.

parts.title: How the Church Learned to Tell the Story
parts.body:
The church grasped early that the faith was a story before it was a system, and it fought to keep the story whole against those who would break it. In the second century Irenaeus of Lyons faced the Gnostics, who told a rival story in which the material world was the botched work of a lesser god and salvation meant escaping the body and the creation altogether. Against them Irenaeus recovered the single sweeping drama from creation to consummation, and he gave it a word, recapitulation, his great vision that Christ sums up the whole story in himself, retraces the entire history of the human creature from the beginning, undoing in his obedience what was done in the fall, gathering all things up into himself to heal them. Irenaeus insisted on one God, one creation called good, one continuous story of rescue, and one ending in which the very flesh that fell is raised and the very world that broke is made new. He saved the church from a faith that despises the body and the world, and he did it by refusing to let anyone cut the story into pieces.

Augustine, at the turn of the fifth century, gave the church its grandest reading of the story as the drama of two cities. Watching Rome fall in 410 and the world he knew come apart, he wrote the City of God, tracing the whole human story as the intertwined history of two loves and two cities, the earthly city built on love of self to the contempt of God, and the heavenly city built on love of God to the contempt of self. The two cities run together through all of history, mingled and indistinguishable until the end, and every human life belongs finally to one or the other. Augustine taught the church to read its own moment, even the collapse of an empire, inside the larger story, to see that the City of God outlasts every earthly kingdom and moves steadily toward the restoration where it alone will stand. He gave believers a way to live in turbulent times without despair, as citizens of a city that is coming, sojourners in a story whose ending is sure even when their own age is falling.

The story shaped the worship and the imagination of the whole church through the long centuries. The creeds the church recited are themselves the story in miniature, moving from God the maker of heaven and earth, through the Son born and crucified and risen, to the resurrection of the body and the life of the world to come, so that every believer who confessed the creed was rehearsing the four acts. The church year walked the people through the drama annually, from creation and longing in Advent, through the coming of the rescuer at Christmas, the cross and resurrection at Easter, to the hope of the consummation, training ordinary Christians who could not read to live inside the story by walking through it with their whole bodies year after year. The cathedrals carved the story into stone, creation to fall to judgment to the new creation, so that to walk through the building was to walk through the drama. The church knew that a story is not learned as information but inhabited as a world, and it built its worship to put people inside the story until the story was inside them.

In our own time, against a culture that declared all grand narratives dead, faithful scholars recovered the Bible as the great drama that it is. N. T. Wright argued that Scripture comes to us precisely as a story, an unfinished play in several acts, and that the church's task is to take up its part and improvise faithfully the next scene in continuity with all that has gone before, living as people who know the acts already written and the act still to come. He insisted that the gospel is not the news that we go to heaven when we die but the news that God is reclaiming the whole creation, that resurrection and new creation, not escape, are the story's true ending. Around the same recovery, others worked to put the whole drama back together for ordinary believers fragmented by a faith reduced to private morality, retelling the Scriptures as the single unfolding story of God reclaiming his world, so that Christians could find their own lives located inside it again.

And two thinkers of the age, reading the modern condition from very different angles, made plain why the recovery of the story mattered so urgently. Charles Taylor, in his vast account of how the West became secular, described the modern person as living inside what he called the immanent frame, a closed world with no window to anything beyond it, a flattened story in which the transcendent has been bracketed out and meaning must be manufactured from within. Taylor showed that this frame is not the simple truth that finally dawned but one contestable story among others, a particular way of imagining the world that we have come to mistake for reality itself, and that the haunting many moderns feel, the sense that the closed frame is not the whole truth, is the pressure of a larger story leaking back in. Alasdair MacIntyre, surveying the wreckage of modern moral life, argued that a human being is essentially a storytelling creature, that I can only answer the question what am I to do if I can answer the prior question of what story I find myself a part of, and that the disorientation of modern ethics is precisely the disorientation of people who have lost the story that once made their lives intelligible. Between them they named the disease with great precision, a culture trying to live in a closed frame and a fragmented people who no longer know what story they are in, and in naming it they pointed straight back to the thing the church had been carrying all along, the true and unbroken drama large enough to live inside.

parts.title: Knowledge Tested Against Scripture
parts.body: The human need for story, meaning, and a frame to live inside has been studied closely by philosophers, psychologists, and scholars of narrative, and much of what they have found is true and confirms what Scripture always assumed about the storytelling creature. All truth is God's truth, and the church can learn from honest observers of how human beings make sense of their lives. But every account of meaning and story carries a buried picture of what a person is and whether there is a true story at all, and that picture has to be tested. What follows takes several bodies of secular insight seriously, names what each sees clearly, and weighs each against Scripture.

secular.author: Jean-Francois Lyotard and the postmodern critique
secular.whatItGetsRight: Lyotard famously defined the postmodern condition as incredulity toward metanarratives, the grand stories of progress, reason, and emancipation that the modern age told about itself, and the critique landed real blows. Those secular grand narratives had indeed been used to oppress, to justify conquest and erase difference, to baptize the powerful, and the suspicion that a totalizing story can become a tool of domination is a warning worth heeding. The critique rightly exposed the pretensions of the modern myths of inevitable human progress, which had promised a heaven they could not deliver and left a century of blood.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: The critique exposes the false grand narratives and then overreaches, concluding that because the modern myths failed, all overarching stories must be illusions, leaving people with only fragments and local tales. Scripture answers that the cure for a false story is not no story but the true one, and that the gospel is the one grand narrative immune to the critique, because its hero does not seize power but is crucified by it, its story exalts the lowly and welcomes the outsider, and its ending is not an empire but a wedding feast. The critique is right that a story can become a weapon. The gospel is the story whose center is a Lamb, and it cannot be made into one without ceasing to be itself.

secular.author: Dan McAdams and narrative psychologists
secular.whatItGetsRight: The research on narrative identity has shown, with decades of careful study, that human beings construct their very selves through story, that we make sense of our lives by weaving our experiences into an internalized and evolving narrative with a past, a present, and an imagined future, and that the coherence and redemptive shape of a person's life story predicts their psychological health. People who can frame their lives as a meaningful story, especially one in which suffering leads somewhere, flourish in ways that the storyless do not. This is a striking empirical confirmation that we are, at the deepest level, narrative creatures who cannot live well without a story.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: The research demonstrates that we live by story and treats the story chiefly as something the self constructs and revises for its own coherence, a useful fiction the mind assembles. Scripture agrees that we are storytelling creatures and insists the story we most need is not one we author but one we are written into, true whether or not it comforts us. A self-constructed narrative can collapse the moment reality refuses to fit it, and the man who has built his own redemptive story has no answer when the redemption does not come. The believer's story holds under the same blows because its author is not the self but God, and its redemptive ending is not a hopeful frame the mind imposes but a future the risen Christ has secured.

secular.source: Man's Search for Meaning and the will to meaning
secular.author: Viktor Frankl
secular.whatItGetsRight: Frankl, out of the Nazi camps, established with unforgettable force that the human being's deepest drive is not pleasure or power but meaning, that a person can endure almost any suffering if it is set within a meaning, and that those who lost the sense that their lives meant something perished while those who held a why to live could bear almost any how. He showed that meaning is not a luxury but a survival need, that the will to meaning is the central fact of the human person, and that a life with no meaning to frame its suffering is a life that breaks.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Frankl proves that we cannot live without meaning and locates the source of meaning finally in the individual's freedom to choose an attitude, a meaning the self supplies to its own circumstances. Scripture honors that freedom and grounds meaning somewhere sturdier than the self's own choosing, in a story that is objectively true, a creation that is actually good, a redemption that has actually happened, an ending that is actually coming. Frankl's meaning, heroic as it is, must be generated by the sufferer out of his own resolve and can run dry when the resolve fails. The believer's meaning is received, not generated, anchored in what God has done and will do, and so it holds even when the sufferer himself has nothing left to supply.

secular.source: The Denial of Death and the terror beneath culture
secular.author: Ernest Becker
secular.whatItGetsRight: Becker argued, in a work that has shaped a whole field, that human culture is at bottom a vast set of hero systems, immortality projects by which mortal creatures try to feel that their brief lives are significant and will outlast death, and that the terror of our own finitude drives nearly everything we build and believe. He saw with rare clarity that human beings cannot bear the thought of meaningless death, that we are creatures who need our lives to count against the void, and that much of our striving is a flight from the grave we cannot face.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Becker diagnoses the terror of death and the desperate human hunger for a story that defeats it, and concludes that every such story is finally an illusion, a brave lie the creature tells itself against the dark. Scripture agrees that we cannot bear meaningless death and that our immortality projects are idols, and then says the thing Becker could not, that the hunger for a death-defeating story is not a delusion to be managed but a signal of the story that is actually true. The empty tomb is not another hero system. It is the one place where the human terror of death meets, not a comforting illusion, but a man who walked out of his grave, and the believer's hope against death is not a lie he tells the void but a fact the void could not hold.

secular.source: The anthropology of myth and the structure of story
secular.author: Joseph Campbell and the comparative mythologists
secular.whatItGetsRight: Campbell and the comparative study of myth documented that the great stories of humanity share a common shape, the pattern of departure, ordeal, death, and return, the hero who goes down into the dark and comes back transformed, and that this deep structure recurs across cultures that never met. The work reveals a profound truth, that the human imagination everywhere reaches for the same shape of story, a fall and a rescue, a death and a rising, as though that shape were written into us, the form our hearts expect a true story to take.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Campbell saw the recurring shape clearly and concluded that the gospel is simply one more instance of the universal myth, the same eternal pattern dressed in Jewish clothing, true only as the others are, on the inside, as psychology. Scripture turns the observation the other way. The reason every culture half-remembers a dying and rising hero is that the human heart was made for the true one, and the gospel is the myth become fact, the pattern all the others were dreaming finally happening in real history, under a named governor, outside a real city, in a tomb that was actually empty. The other stories are echoes and longings. This one is the event the echoes were echoing, and it asks not to be admired as a pattern but believed as a fact.

parts.title: Where Faithful Christians Differ
parts.body: Believers who share the same Scripture and the same conviction that we live inside the one great drama still differ over how to live in the overlap between the acts, between the redemption already begun and the restoration not yet come. It runs to how much weight to give the already and how much to the not-yet, how present the kingdom is and how far off. Hear each emphasis at its strongest, because both are reading the same story, and both are guarding against a real danger.

views.view: Emphasizing the already, the kingdom breaking in now
views.body: This emphasis presses the truth that redemption has genuinely begun, that with the death and resurrection of Christ the new creation has actually broken into the present age, and that the believer is called to live now as a citizen of the world that is coming and an agent of its arrival. Christ is risen, the Spirit is poured out, the kingdom is among us, and the powers of the age to come are already at work in those who believe. This emphasis takes seriously that the redemption of act three is not merely the rescue of souls for a future heaven but the reclaiming of the whole creation, begun now, so that the church is called to push back the effects of the fall in real and visible ways, to heal, to make peace, to do justice, to bring the patterns of the coming restoration into the present world as signs that the King has come. Advocates point to the resurrection appearances, to the miracles of the kingdom, to the early church turning the world upside down, and they insist that a faith which postpones all renewal to the far future has quietly surrendered the present age to the powers and reduced the gospel to an escape plan. The danger they are guarding against is real, a passive and world-abandoning Christianity that shrugs at injustice and decay because it expects to leave it all behind, that does nothing to anticipate the kingdom because it has located the kingdom entirely in the beyond. Against that, they hold that the risen Christ is making all things new beginning now, and that the believer is summoned to live and work as though the restoration has already started, because it has.

views.view: Emphasizing the not-yet, the restoration still to come
views.body: This emphasis presses the truth that the story is not finished, that we live in a world still groaning under the fall, still subject to death and decay, still awaiting a restoration that has not arrived, and that the believer is called to a patient and hopeful waiting rather than a triumphant claiming. The kingdom has come, yes, but in hiddenness, like a seed, like leaven, and its fullness lies on the far side of the return of Christ and the resurrection of the dead. This emphasis takes seriously that the present age remains genuinely fallen, that Christians still sicken and grieve and die, that injustice persists and the new creation is not yet visible in power, and it warns against the disappointment and disillusion that come when believers expect more of the already than the story actually promises now. Advocates point to the groaning of creation that Paul says awaits its redemption, to the apostles who still suffered and died, to the long New Testament posture of hope deferred and patient endurance, and they insist that a faith which over-realizes the kingdom, claiming a present victory the story reserves for the end, sets people up for a crushing fall when the healing does not come and the world does not bend. The danger they are guarding against is also real, a presumptuous and brittle Christianity that promises triumph now, that tells the suffering their pain only proves a lack of faith, that mistakes the overlap for the ending and breaks when reality refuses to cooperate. Against that, they hold that we live between the acts in hope and not yet in sight, laboring faithfully while we wait for the restoration that only the returning Christ will bring, and that the deepest faith is the patience that trusts the ending it cannot yet see.

parts.title: What Living Inside the Story Forms in You
parts.body:
You cannot truly come to live inside the four-act story without being changed by it, because a story you actually inhabit reshapes how you see everything, and God, who gave us the drama and not merely a set of doctrines, means the story itself to be a chief instrument of our formation. The person who has only the verses stays fragmented, his life a pile of unconnected episodes. The person who has entered the story finds his whole existence slowly gathered into a single coherent shape, and the gathering changes him.

It forms in you a deep gratitude that no setback can fully erase, because the story begins with the goodness of creation and you never lose the memory of act one. The person who believes the world is an accident has nothing to be grateful to and no one to thank, and his pleasures float free of any giver. The person who lives inside the story receives the whole world as a gift, the bread and the body and the work and the morning light all charged with the goodness of the One who made them very good, and gratitude becomes the settled atmosphere of his life rather than an occasional feeling. He can taste the gift because he knows the Giver, and even in a fallen world the original goodness keeps breaking through to a heart trained to receive it.

It forms an honest realism that does not flinch from the brokenness, because the story includes the fall and refuses to pretend. The person living by the thin optimism of the age must keep insisting that everything is fine and is undone the moment it plainly is not. The person who lives inside the four acts has a place for the ruin, knows that the world is genuinely broken and his own heart with it, and so he does not have to deny the grief, the injustice, the decay, or his own sin. He can look the darkness full in the face without despair, because he knows which act he is in, that the fall is real and is not the last word, and this honesty is its own kind of strength, the strength of a man who does not have to lie about how bad it is because he knows the story does not end there.

It forms a resilient hope that the worst circumstance cannot reach, because the story moves through redemption toward restoration and the believer knows where it is going. The person with no story, or with the thin one, faces the grave and the diagnosis with nothing but a brave face over an abyss. The person who lives inside the drama faces the same grave knowing it is a comma and not a period, that act four is coming, that the body will be raised and the world made new and every tear wiped away, and so his hope is not optimism about his circumstances but certainty about the ending. He can lose much and not be destroyed, because the story has an ending he did not invent and cannot lose, secured by a Christ who has already walked out of his own tomb.

And it forms, beneath all of it, a self that is finally integrated rather than fragmented, which is the formation the whole drama is for. The person living storyless lives in pieces, his work and faith and suffering and body all disconnected. The person who has come to live inside the true story finds every piece located, his work as part of the keeping of creation, his suffering as a chapter inside the act of rescue, his body as a thing made good and destined to be raised, his death as the door into restoration, his whole small life written into the great one whose center is Christ. He is no longer a character improvising in the dark, unsure what play he is in. He knows the acts already written and the act still to come, he knows his place and his part, and a life that knows its story is a life that holds together, integrated not by his own effort to assemble it but by the One who has gathered all things, including him, into himself.

parts.title: Practice
parts.body: You do not come to live inside the story by agreeing that it is true. You come to live inside it by small, repeated acts of rehearsing it, locating your life within it, and learning to see everything through it, over years, under grace. None of what follows will move the story from your head to your bones overnight, and that is not how a story becomes the world you live in. It happens by inhabiting it until it inhabits you. Begin with one thing, this week, and let the rest come as the story takes hold.

steps: Name, in one honest paragraph, the story you have actually been living by, the thin one the culture handed you, and notice where it fails to carry the weight of your real life. You cannot move into the true story until you see the borrowed one you have been living in.

Read the four acts straight through this week, the opening chapters of Genesis for creation and fall, a Gospel for redemption, and the closing chapters of Revelation for restoration, in one or two sittings, to feel the shape of the whole drama rather than the pieces.

Take the one part of your life that feels most meaningless right now and locate it inside the story. Ask which act your pain or your work belongs to, and let the frame begin to hold what felt like a disconnected fragment.
Pray a single line from the ending over your week, that God is making all things new, and let the certainty of act four loosen your grip on the fear that this broken act is the last one.

Learn the four acts well enough to tell the whole story in your own words in two minutes, creation, fall, redemption, restoration, with Christ at the center. A story you can tell is a story you have begun to inhabit, and a story you cannot tell is one you only half believe.

Recite a creed slowly, as the story in miniature, and watch it walk from God the maker through the crucified and risen Son to the resurrection of the body and the life of the world to come. Let the old words rehearse the four acts into you week by week.

Read one passage you know well and ask which act it is set in and how it serves the whole drama. Practice reading Scripture as a story going somewhere rather than a quarry of detached verses, until the plot starts to appear.

Take one fragmented area of your life, your work or your money or your body, and write how it looks inside each act, good in creation, broken in the fall, being redeemed now, destined for restoration. Watch a disconnected piece find its place in the whole.

Walk through the church year, or build your own rhythm through it, letting Advent rehearse the longing, Christmas the coming, Easter the turning, and the long hope of the consummation train your body to live through the acts and not only to know them.

Wrestle honestly with the overlap, the already and the not-yet, in the part of your life where you are waiting on God. Decide where you are tempted to over-claim the already or to lose hope in the not-yet, and let the story correct the imbalance.

Read a faithful retelling of the whole biblical drama, the work of those who have put the story back together for fragmented believers, and let someone help you see the single sweep of it from the first sentence to the last vision.

Practice seeing your suffering through the story this season. When the hard thing comes, locate it, name the act, and refuse both the lie that says the brokenness is final and the lie that says it is not real. Let the story carry what the thin story could not.

Let the story become the lens you see everything through, until your work, your marriage, your money, your body, and your death are no longer separate problems but chapters of one drama, and your life ceases to be a pile of episodes and becomes a single coherent whole.

Live your part faithfully in the act we are in, improvising the next scene in continuity with all that has gone before, neither retreating from a fallen world nor pretending it is already healed, but laboring in hope as one who knows the acts already written and the act still to come.

Hand the story on. Tell it to your children, your friends, the skeptic who has run out of his own story, not as a doctrine to affirm but as the true drama large enough to live inside, and become for someone else the one who shows where their fragmented life belongs.

Keep returning to the One who is the story's center, until knowing the drama and knowing him have become the same thing. Read the whole Bible for the rest of your life not as a manual to master but as the story you are written into, whose author and hero and ending is Christ, until your own small life is so gathered into his great one that you can face the last act unafraid, certain of the world made new and the dwelling of God with man, where the story has no end and no one is fragmented and every character is finally, fully home.
